Como $m(x)$ es irreducible, los 256 byte: Since $m(x)$ is irreducible, the 256 bytes form a field, $\text{GF}(2^8)$: everything that is not zero has an inverse, $a^{-1} = a^{254}$.
Con $m(x)$ irreducible, los 256 bytes co: With $m(x)$ irreducible, the 256 bytes with this addition and this product form a field: you can add, subtract (which is adding), multiply and divide by any non-zero byte, and all the usual rules hold. It is called $\text{GF}(2^8)$, the Galois field of 256 elements, and it is the exact analogue of the integers modulo a prime, with $m(x)$ in the prime's role. There is only one version of this field, up to the naming of its elements; AES chose $m(x)$ among the 30 irreducible polynomials of degree 8 because it was the first on the list.

Évariste Galois describió los cuerpos fi: Évariste Galois described finite fields in 1830, at twenty, in a work the Paris Academy of Sciences mislaid; he died in a duel two years later, after spending the previous night writing his results out in letters. Irving Reed and Gustave Solomon used these fields in 1960 to correct errors, and Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen put them at the centre of Rijndael in 1998. The polynomial $x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1$ was chosen, according to its authors, for being the first irreducible one of degree 8 in a table in a textbook.
